title: ZhenFund's Handover: After Xu Xiaoping Steps Back, Partners Can't Tax the Young
dek: ZhenFund fights the erosion of its first-generation edge with all-hands sourcing and per-project individual ownership — every logo hangs under one name, and partners can't coast on decision-making alone.
why: High information density and lots of mechanism detail: how the IC votes, why partners can't levy a tax, why executive founders are dangerous. Suited to anyone curious about VC organizational design.
who: Founders, investors and fund LPs curious about VC organizational design and handover mechanisms, especially those watching generational succession in Chinese venture capital.
skip: The song and self-introduction at the start, 0:00-2:02, and the chat about artsy youth and entrepreneurship at 1:04:34-1:07:34.

points.body: In 2018 Xu Xiaoping began attending only half the investment committee meetings, but nobody knew which half — Fang Aizhi's phrasing is "you might see Teacher Xu today, you might not." By 2020 he took no part in any deal-level discussion at all, not even the weekly meeting. Liu Yan says this exit was "really very thorough," and not a sudden impulse: from very early on, Xu Xiaoping and Wang Qiang repeatedly said "after another couple of funds, this fund is yours." Liu Yan says he heard it for eight years. This kind of handover — planned years in advance, pulled back step by step — has almost no precedent among China's top-tier funds.

points.h: ZhenFund's IC doesn't decide by partner vote count
points.body: At nearly every Chinese VC the IC is made up of partners and only partners vote; Liu Yan calls ZhenFund "the only outlier": analysts through partners all take part, each person gets one vote, and votes aren't tallied. The decision comes down to who holds a strong opinion about the project — if both Anna and Yusen like it, it's a yes; if one likes it and one doesn't, they look to other colleagues; if everyone dislikes it, it depends on how strong the conviction of the colleague pushing the project is. Someone will say "I wouldn't invest, but I also wouldn't block this project." Only recently did they start using anonymous Feishu voting, and only to keep track, not as a decision standard.

points.h: Partners can't levy a tax on the young
points.body: From day one ZhenFund has insisted partners source deals themselves: every month each person has to submit a table of the projects they sourced, and Anna has to write one and tick the boxes too. A colleague said straight out in a meeting that Anna hadn't looked at many projects that month and surely didn't know that sector well. Back when Xu Xiaoping was still around he said that if one day ZhenFund's partners only made decisions and let the young people go find projects, "ZhenFund is finished." Liu Yan's summary is "you partners can't tax the young" — levying a tax means degeneration. The old partner Zhaoyu complained before leaving: if you can't tax and you forever have to hunt for projects, what's the point of being a partner.

points.h: Each project hangs under exactly one name
points.body: On ZhenFund's website and in its fundraising decks, every project has only one person's ownership, occasionally two, but for eighty or ninety percent it's one person — whether that person is an analyst, an investment manager or a partner. Xiaohongshu is Anna's, Party Animals is Yusen's, a certain Mendan is Liu Yan's. Tianjie, whom Liu Yan recruited, invested in a biotech project; Liu Yan invested in it too, but "his project is his, my project is mine" — Liu Yan never knows the data on Tianjie's project. This structure lets young colleagues truly own a deal, and it also means partners can't skim a cut off the young.

points.h: ZhenFund's methodology is incompatible with other funds
points.body: Liu Yan says ZhenFund's core philosophy of judging people is actually hard for someone trained at another fund to agree with — everyone else looks at how big the market is, compares how many companies are in the sector, who's number one; ZhenFund doesn't think that way. Someone from Sequoia can adapt quickly at IDG or Hillhouse, but ZhenFund's methodology may be at odds with those from the ground up. The philosophical split is this: is your judgment of the market more accurate, or is a good founder's judgment of the market more accurate. So ZhenFund tends to grow people from a blank sheet; Xu Xiaoping's slogan is "faith makes it work" — believe in the founder, and internally you also have to believe in this business of betting on people. In ten years only three colleagues left for other funds.

points.h: Professors who don't found full-time do better
points.body: ZhenFund studied every listed company in China and every company founded successfully by a professor, sorting professors into those who served as CEO themselves, those whose PhD student was CEO, and those merely lending their name. The conclusion overturned the received view: the most successful projects weren't professors founding full-time, but professors not full-time and students full-time. Liu Yan stresses this isn't necessarily causal — it's not that a professor coming out is bad, but that in many cases the professor had no choice about coming out and the company still made it. So ZhenFund is now more tolerant about whether a professor is full-time, and looks more at whether the student is full-time and is CEO. Another finding: the golden age for founding is roughly 26 or 28, but if you take all A-share listed companies rather than just internet ones, 35 becomes the main standard.

points.h: Executive founders have the lowest success rate
points.body: Liu Yan says that across four quadrants, executive founders have the lowest success rate, because "the best founders don't go become executives." ZhenFund started systematically hunting executives in 2016-2018, and by 2020 realized the whole executive cohort was dangerous. The reason: someone who chooses to be an executive is essentially risk-averse, and finding a risk-taker among the risk-averse is harder. Executive founders are the hardest to judge, because with platform amplification it's very hard to separate the platform's advantage from their own. Now zero-to-one founding experience is strongly preferred, and a big-tech background has instead become a disadvantage you have to explain. But this isn't an absolute theory — Shen Peng fought the delivery war inside Meituan, Wang Xiaofeng and Kate ran a city at Uber, and both got funded.

points.h: Once the first-generation edge is gone, only a system can fight back
points.body: Liu Yan says Xu Xiaoping back then held something close to the martial-arts overlord's position among early angels — with Teacher Xu making the approach, they could even get a cheaper price than others. Today those first-generation advantages are gone, "we're using a system to fight back." He tells a story that hit him hard: while competing for a project, Tina, who had risen from intern to director, faced a rival fund whose big name went to pitch in person, and the founder said he wouldn't let ZhenFund invest. Tina asked Teacher Xu to step in — in 2015-2016 this was an invincible move, like carrying the Ark of the Covenant into battle. But that time Teacher Xu refused Tina; the moment the call connected Tina burst into tears, and Xu spent forty minutes telling her why he was no longer needed, like a teacher or a father saying "you have to get used to days without me."

quotes.text: He's just a Schrödinger's appearance. We hold the investment committee every Tuesday. He can — half the time he won't come. And you don't know whether he's coming today or not.
We can never let partners live in comfort and privilege, sitting there only making decisions — because we don't think decisions are the hardest part of this industry.
Things that do you no harm and do others good — do as many of them as you can.
It was really like a teacher, or a father: you have to get used to days without me.
